At 4:17 every morning, the town’s streetlights blinked off in sequence, beginning at the river and climbing toward the hills. No one had programmed them to do this. The municipal electrician had checked the timers, replaced the relays, and once, in frustration, disconnected the entire system. Still, at 4:17, the lamps went dark one by one, as if an invisible hand were pinching out a row of candles.

Most people slept through it.

Mara did not.

She worked nights at the bakery on Bell Street, shaping dough while the ovens breathed heat into the blue-black hours. By four, the first loaves were cooling on wire racks, their crusts ticking softly. Mara would carry a cup of coffee to the front window and watch the darkness descend.

First the lamp beside the river.

Then the one outside the pharmacy.

Then the square, the church steps, the abandoned cinema, and finally the steep road leading north.

Seven seconds after the last light vanished, they all returned at once.

Mara had timed it.

She had also noticed something else.

During those seven seconds, a door appeared across the street.

It stood between the laundromat and a narrow brick building, where there was ordinarily only a graffiti-covered wall. The door was tall, painted green, and fitted with a brass handle polished by hands that could not possibly have touched it. A small white card was pinned at eye level.

Mara could not read it from the bakery.

For three weeks, she watched the door appear and disappear. Each morning she promised herself she would cross the street. Each morning the lamps went out, and for seven seconds she remained frozen behind the glass.

Seven seconds was not long.

It was long enough to make a choice, but not long enough to make it carefully.

On the twenty-second morning, Mara put down her coffee before 4:17. She removed her apron, opened the bakery door, and stood at the curb.

The lamps began to fail.

River.

Pharmacy.

Square.

Church.

Cinema.

Hill.

Darkness.

Mara ran.

The door waited, green and impossible. She reached it with perhaps three seconds left. The card read:

FOR THOSE WHO MISPLACED SOMETHING IMPORTANT.

Mara seized the handle.

The streetlights flashed back on.

She was no longer standing on Bell Street.

She found herself inside a vast room crowded with shelves. They rose higher than trees and extended beyond sight, filled not with books or boxes, but with lost things.

Single gloves.

Unsent letters.

Keys with no remembered locks.

Names forgotten moments after introductions.

Umbrellas abandoned on trains.

Childhood summers, preserved in jars like golden fruit.

Courage that had failed at the decisive instant.

Songs heard once through an open window.

There were wedding rings, train tickets, tempers, opportunities, and thousands upon thousands of hours.

A man sat behind a desk beneath a green-shaded lamp. He wore a gray suit and a badge that said ATTENDANT.

“You’re early,” he said.

“For what?”

“Most people don’t find us until much later.”

Mara looked behind her. The door was gone.

“I have to get back. The morning baker arrives at five.”

“Everyone has to get back,” the attendant said. “Eventually.”

He opened a ledger. Its pages were thin and densely written.

“Name?”

“Mara Vale.”

His finger traveled down a column. “You’ve lost thirty-seven hairpins, eleven recipes, one silver earring, a library card, your ability to whistle, and approximately six months to a man called Daniel.”

“That sounds low.”

“We only count unrecoverable time.”

Mara folded her arms. “I didn’t come for any of those.”

“No,” said the attendant. “People rarely know what they came for.”

He led her between the shelves. As they walked, objects whispered from their places. A red mitten called for a child now in his seventies. A cracked compass insisted north had moved. Somewhere above, a telephone rang unanswered.

They stopped before a glass cabinet.

Inside was a small paper boat.

Mara stared at it.

The boat had been folded from pale blue stationery. One side bore three words in her mother’s handwriting:

When you’re ready.

Mara had not seen it in twenty years.

Her mother had made paper boats during the summer she was ill. She folded them from bills, recipes, envelopes, anything within reach, and set them along the windowsill. On the last morning, she asked Mara to choose one.

Mara, sixteen and furious at the entire machinery of the world, had refused.

After the funeral, the boats were gone.

“What’s inside?” Mara asked.

The attendant shrugged. “It belongs to you.”

She opened the cabinet and lifted the boat. The paper felt warm. With careful fingers she unfolded it.

There was no secret message. No final wisdom. No explanation for suffering.

Only a grocery list.

Milk. Apples. Cinnamon. Flour.

And beneath it:

Mara likes the bread with too much sugar.

She laughed once, sharply, and then began to cry.

The attendant looked away with the practiced courtesy of someone who had witnessed every possible grief.

“I thought I’d lost what she wanted to tell me,” Mara said.

“You did.”

“This is just a grocery list.”

“Yes.”

“I already knew she loved me.”

“Knowing is a thing people misplace every day.”

Mara pressed the paper against her chest.

“Can I take it?”

“Nothing leaves here unchanged.”

“What does that mean?”

“It means you may take the object, but not the years you spent without it. You may recover the words, but not the voice. You may find what was lost, but finding is not the same as undoing.”

“I’ll take it anyway.”

The attendant smiled. “They usually do.”

A green door appeared at the end of the aisle.

When Mara stepped through, she was standing across from the bakery. The streetlights were still bright. Only seven seconds had passed.

Inside, the loaves waited on their racks.

At dawn, Mara baked a batch of bread with too much sugar. She set the first loaf in the window, though she could not have said for whom.

The next morning, at 4:17, the streetlights did not go out.

They never did again.

But sometimes, just before sunrise, Mara noticed people pausing beside the brick wall across the street. They would touch the graffiti as if searching for a handle. Some carried photographs. Some carried nothing.

Mara never told them what she had found.

She simply opened the bakery early and gave them something warm for the road.
